title: Microeconomics for Finance
text:
This course provides students with relevant microeconomic methods to tackle finance issues. The course covers 24 hours of material and is designed for first-year Master in Finance students at Paris Dauphine University - PSL.


The course consists of four main topics:

Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy - Understanding how markets allocate resources through voluntary exchange
Decision Making under Uncertainty - Expected utility theory and risk preferences
Equilibrium in Markets for Securities - Asset pricing and portfolio theory
Investment Decisions under Market Imperfections - Asymmetric information and agency problems






Topic 1: Exchange Economy
Understanding the fundamentals of market equilibrium with a focus on exchange between agents.


Topic 2: Decision under Uncertainty
Expected utility theory, risk aversion, and portfolio choice.


Topic 3: Securities Markets
Asset pricing models, CAPM, and market equilibrium concepts.


Topic 4: Market Imperfections
Asymmetric information, principal-agent problems, and real-world market frictions.






Instructor: Juan F. Imbet
Institution: Paris Dauphine University - PSL
Level: Master in Finance, 1st Year
Duration: 24 hours
Evaluation: Mid-term and final exams




By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Understand the fundamental concepts of microeconomic theory as applied to finance
Analyze market equilibrium under different conditions
Apply expected utility theory to decision-making under uncertainty
Comprehend asset pricing models and their implications
Recognize the impact of market imperfections on investment decisions





Basic knowledge of microeconomics
Familiarity with mathematical concepts (calculus, probability)
Understanding of financial instruments


This course builds upon the foundational work of previous instructors while incorporating modern developments in financial economics.

text:
Juan F. Imbet
Assistant Professor
Department of Finance
Paris Dauphine University - PSL



This 24-hour course in Microeconomics for Finance aims to equip students with essential microeconomic tools for analyzing financial markets and decision-making. The course bridges theoretical microeconomics with practical applications in finance.



Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:

Apply microeconomic principles to financial decision-making
Understand market equilibrium concepts in financial contexts
Analyze decision-making under uncertainty using expected utility theory
Comprehend asset pricing models and their implications
Recognize the impact of market imperfections on investment decisions




The course is divided into four main modules, each building upon the previous one:

Foundation: Exchange economy and basic equilibrium concepts
Risk and Uncertainty: Decision theory and risk preferences
Asset Markets: Pricing and portfolio theory
Real-World Applications: Market imperfections and agency problems




All course materials are provided in interactive HTML format using Quarto and Reveal.js, allowing for an engaging learning experience with embedded mathematical expressions and visualizations.



For questions about the course content or materials, please contact the instructor.

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Adam and Bob are the only two individuals in an island. Adam has been able to collect 10 coconuts and 5 fish, while Bob has 5 coconuts and 10 fish. Both individuals have the same utility function over coconut and fish consumption bundles represented by the following Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) utility function: \[
u(X_c, X_f) = \left( X_c^{\frac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}} + X_f^{\frac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}} \right)^{\frac{\sigma}{\sigma - 1}},
\qquad \sigma=2,
\] where \(X_c\) is the number of coconuts and \(X_f\) the number of fish.

Compute the Marshallian demand functions for coconuts and fish for both Adam and Bob as a function of prices.

Compute the equilibrium prices of coconuts and fish in this economy.

Compute the equilibrium consumption bundles for both Adam and Bob.

For an arbitrary level \(\bar{u}\) of utility, compute the Hicksian demand functions for both Adam and Bob as a function of prices and utility.

Compute the expenditure function as a function of prices and utility.

Show that Marshallian and Hicksian demands coincide when utility is set to the Marshallian utility level.





Only one hospital in a country provides medical services. Cities have preferences over medical services \(X\) and cash \(C\): \[
U(X,C) = X^{\frac{1}{2}} C^{\frac{1}{2}}.
\] The government has allocated \(1\) million services to city 1 and \(2\) million to city 2. Cities have no cash. A policy lets cities sell medical services to outside buyers and receive 80% of the market price per service. Normalize the price of cash to \(1\) and let the (producer) price of services be \(p_X\). Compute each city’s optimal \((X,C)\) after the policy.




In the market for tobacco (\(X_t\)) and alcohol (\(X_a\)), Carol and Dave have utilities \[
U_C(X_t, X_a) = X_t^{\frac{1}{3}} X_a^{\frac{2}{3}},\qquad
U_D(X_t, X_a) = X_t^{\frac{2}{3}} X_a^{\frac{1}{3}}.
\] Endowments: Carol \((4,1)\), Dave \((1,4)\).

Compute Marshallian demands.

Find equilibrium prices.

Compute equilibrium consumption bundles.

Suppose a 20% consumption tax on tobacco (buyers pay \((1+\tau)p_t\) with \(\tau=0.2\); sellers receive \(p_t\)).


Characterize an equilibrium with the tax and lump-sum transfers \((T_C,T_D)\) such that markets clear.


Give one revenue-neutral example with \(T_C+T_D\) equal to tax revenue and compute the resulting prices and allocations.


If the government rebated revenue equally, what are the transfers?







Apples (\(X_A\)) and pears (\(X_P\)) are traded by Eve and Frank. Block pricing applies to purchases: first \(\bar{A}\) apples at price \(\bar p_a\), additional apples at \(\bar p_a/2\); analogously, first \(\bar P\) pears at price \(\bar p_p\), additional pears at \(\bar p_p/2\). Eve’s endowment \((\omega_{EA},\omega_{EP})\), Frank’s \((\omega_{FA},\omega_{FP})\). Both have Cobb–Douglas utility \[
U(X_A,X_P)=X_A^\alpha X_P^{1-\alpha},\qquad \alpha\in(0,1).
\]

Write each consumer’s piecewise-linear budget and the corresponding Marshallian demand case by case.

State market-clearing conditions and characterize equilibrium prices.

Characterize equilibrium allocations.

Comparative statics: how do equilibrium prices/allocations change as \(\bar A\) and \(\bar P\) increase?





Two-good \((1,2)\), two-consumer \((A,B)\) exchange economy with initial allocations \[
\omega_A=(4,2),\qquad \omega_B=(2,4),
\] total endowments \((6,6)\). Both have \(U(X_1,X_2)=X_1^\alpha X_2^{1-\alpha}\).

Draw an Edgeworth box (\(6\times 6\)) and locate the initial endowment.

Draw budget lines through the endowment for each consumer.

Draw indifference curves for \(A\) and discuss their shape.

What is the slope of a budget line?

Compute equilibrium relative prices and show the equilibrium allocation.

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Solution to Exercise 1

Step 0) Simplify the utility with an increasing transformation
With \(\sigma=2\), \[
u(X_c,X_f)=(X_c^{1/2}+X_f^{1/2})^2.
\] Apply the strictly increasing transformation \(g(u)=\sqrt{u}\): \[
\tilde u(X_c,X_f)=\sqrt{u(X_c,X_f)}=X_c^{1/2}+X_f^{1/2}.
\] This preserves preferences (same optima) and makes derivatives simple. It is linear in the transformed consumptions \(Z_c=\sqrt{X_c}\) and \(Z_f=\sqrt{X_f}\), which makes the MRS and the FOCs very easy.


1) Marshallian demands (for any consumer with income \(I\) and prices \((p_c,p_f)\))
With \(\tilde u=\sqrt{X_c}+\sqrt{X_f}\), the FOC at an interior optimum sets MRS equal to the price ratio: \[
\text{MRS}_{c,f}
=\frac{\partial \tilde u/\partial X_c}{\partial \tilde u/\partial X_f}
=\frac{\tfrac{1}{2}X_c^{-1/2}}{\tfrac{1}{2}X_f^{-1/2}}
=\left(\frac{X_f}{X_c}\right)^{1/2}
=\frac{p_c}{p_f}.
\] Hence \(X_f=X_c\left(\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2\). With the budget \(p_c X_c+p_f X_f=I\), solve: \[
X_c^M=\frac{I\,p_f}{p_c(p_c+p_f)},
\qquad
X_f^M=\frac{I\,p_c}{p_f(p_c+p_f)}.
\] Individual incomes from endowments: \[
I_A=10p_c+5p_f,\qquad I_B=5p_c+10p_f.
\] Plug these into the formulas above for Adam and Bob.


2) Equilibrium prices
Normalize \(p_c=1\) and let \(p_f=p\). Aggregate endowments: \((15,15)\). Market-clearing for coconuts: \[
\begin{aligned}
X_{c,A}^M+X_{c,B}^M=\frac{(10+5p)p}{1+p}+\frac{(5+10p)p}{1+p}
=\frac{(15+15p)p}{1+p}&=15 \\
\Rightarrow\quad (15+15p)p&=15(1+p) \\
\Rightarrow\quad 15p^2&=15 \\
\Rightarrow\quad p^2&=1 \\
\Rightarrow\quad p&=1.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus \(p_c=p_f=1\). Why don’t we normalize with the simplex \(p_c+p_f=1\)? Look at the expression and choose the normalization that makes the algebra easiest.


3) Equilibrium allocations
With \(p_c=p_f=1\), \(I_A=I_B=15\) and \[
X_{c,i}^M=X_{f,i}^M=\frac{I_i}{2}=\frac{15}{2}=7.5,\quad i\in\{A,B\}.
\]


4) Hicksian (compensated) demands
Cost-minimization \(\min_{h_c,h_f}\{p_c h_c+p_f h_f \text{.  s.t.}\ (h_c^{1/2}+h_f^{1/2})^2\ge \bar u\}\) is equivalent to \(h_c^{1/2}+h_f^{1/2}\ge \bar u^{1/2}\). The solution yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L} &=p_c h_c+p_f h_f+\mu\big(\bar u^{1/2}-(h_c^{1/2}+h_f^{1/2})\big) \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h_c} &=p_c - \mu \frac{1}{2} h_c^{-1/2}=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu=2 p_c h_c^{1/2}, \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h_f} &=p_f - \mu \frac{1}{2} h_f^{-1/2}=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu=2 p_f h_f^{1/2} \\
\Rightarrow\quad 2 p_c h_c^{1/2} &= 2 p_f h_f^{1/2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad h_f = h_c \left(\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2.
\end{aligned}
\] Replace into the utility constraint (Local Non-Satiation ensures equality): \[
\begin{aligned}
h_c^{1/2}+h_f^{1/2} &= \bar u^{1/2} \\
h_c^{1/2}+\left(\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right) h_c^{1/2} &= \bar u^{1/2} \\
h_c^{1/2}\left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right) &= \bar u^{1/2} \\
h_c^{1/2} &= \frac{\bar u^{1/2}}{1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}} \\
h_c &= \frac{\bar u}{\left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly for \(h_f\): \[
h_f = \frac{\bar u}{\left(1+\frac{p_f}{p_c}\right)^2}.
\]


5) Expenditure function
The expenditure function is \[
\begin{aligned}
e(p_c,p_f,\bar u) &= p_c h_c + p_f h_f \\
&= \frac{p_c \bar u}{\left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2} + \frac{p_f \bar u}{\left(1+\frac{p_f}{p_c}\right)^2} \\
&= \bar u \cdot \left( \frac{p_c}{\left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2} + \frac{p_f}{\left(1+\frac{p_f}{p_c}\right)^2} \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
or simplified: \[
\begin{aligned}
e(p_c,p_f,\bar u) &= \bar u \cdot \left( \frac{p_c}{\left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2} + \frac{p_f}{\left(1+\frac{p_f}{p_c}\right)^2} \right) \\
&= \bar u \cdot \left( \frac{p_c p_f^2 + p_f p_c^2}{(p_c+p_f)^2} \right).
\end{aligned}
\]


6) Why Marshallian and Hicksian coincide at the Marshallian utility
In the optimal bundle, budget is spent entirely: \(I=e(p_c,p_f,\bar u)\). Set \(\bar u\) to the Marshallian utility level \(\bar u=u(X_c,X_f)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_c&=\frac{I\,p_f}{p_c(p_c+p_f)} \\
&=\frac{e(p_c,p_f,\bar u)\,p_f}{p_c(p_c+p_f)} \\
&=\frac{\bar u \cdot \left( \frac{p_c p_f^2 + p_f p_c^2}{(p_c+p_f)^2} \right) p_f}{p_c(p_c+p_f)} \\
&= \frac{\bar u (p_c p_f^3 + p_c^2 p_f^2)}{p_c (p_c+p_f)^3} \\
&= \frac{\bar u p_c p_f^2 (p_f + p_c p)}{p_c (p_c+p_f)^3} \\
&=\frac{\bar u \cdot p_f^2}{(p_c+p_f)^2} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
The utility is given by \(\bar u = (X_c^{1/2} + X_f^{1/2})^2\). And only in terms of \(X_c\) we have:
\[
\bar u = (X_c^{1/2} + (X_c\left(\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2)^{1/2})^2
\]
which can be simplified as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bar u &= (X_c^{1/2} + (X_c\left(\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2)^{1/2})^2 \\
&= (X_c^{1/2} + X_c^{1/2}\left(\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right))^2 \\
&= (X_c^{1/2}(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}))^2 \\
&= X_c \cdot \left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Plugin back \[
\begin{aligned}
X_c &= \frac{\bar u \cdot p_f^2}{(p_c+p_f)^2} \\
&= \frac{X_c \cdot \left(1+\frac{p_c}{p_f}\right)^2 \cdot p_f^2}{(p_c+p_f)^2} \\
&= X_c \times \frac{\frac{p_f^2 (p_f+p_c)^2}{p_f^2}}{(p_c+p_f)^2} \\
&= X_c.
\end{aligned}
\]
and same for \(X_f\).

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Solution to Exercise 2
A city with initial services \(X_0\) sells \(s\in[0,X_0]\) units at net price \(0.8\,p_X\) (it keeps 80% of the revenue): \[
X=X_0-s,\qquad C=0.8\,p_X\,s.
\] Maximize \(U=\sqrt{XC}=\sqrt{(X_0-s)(0.8\,p_X\,s)}\).
FOC: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial U}{\partial s} &=-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{0.8\,p_X}{X_0-s}}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{0.8\,p_X (X_0-s)}{s^2}}=0 \\
\Rightarrow\quad -\frac{1}{\sqrt{X_0-s}}+\frac{\sqrt{X_0-s}}{s}&=0 \\
\Rightarrow\quad s&=X_0-s \\
\Rightarrow\quad s&=\frac{X_0}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus each city sells half its initial services, based on their initial endowments. Final consumptions and cash:

City 1: \(X_1=\frac{1}{2}\), \(C_1=0.8\,p_X\cdot \frac{1}{2}=0.4\,p_X\).
City 2: \(X_2=1\), \(C_2=0.8\,p_X\cdot 1=0.8\,p_X\).

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Solution to Exercise 3
Let prices be \((p_t,p_a)\) with \(p_a=1\) (numeraire) and write \(p_t=p\).

1) Marshallian demands
For Cobb–Douglas \(x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\), \[
x^M=\alpha\,\frac{I}{p_x},\qquad y^M=(1-\alpha)\,\frac{I}{p_y}.
\] Incomes from endowments at producer prices: \(I_C=4p+1\), \(I_D=p+4\). Thus \[
\text{Carol }(\alpha=\tfrac13):\quad
X_{t,C}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{I_C}{p},\quad
X_{a,C}=\frac{2}{3} I_C,
\] \[
\text{Dave }(\alpha=\tfrac23):\quad
X_{t,D}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{I_D}{p},\quad
X_{a,D}=\frac{1}{3} I_D.
\]


2) Equilibrium prices (no tax)
Clear tobacco (total endowment \(5\)): \[
\frac{1}{3}\frac{4p+1}{p}+\frac{2}{3}\frac{p+4}{p}=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad p=1.
\] Hence \((p_t,p_a)=(1,1)\).


3) Equilibrium allocations (no tax)
With \(p=1\), incomes \(I_C=I_D=5\): \[
\text{Carol: } \left(X_{t,C},X_{a,C}\right)=\left(\tfrac{5}{3},\,\tfrac{10}{3}\right),\qquad
\text{Dave: } \left(X_{t,D},X_{a,D}\right)=\left(\tfrac{10}{3},\,\tfrac{5}{3}\right).
\]


4) 20% consumption tax on tobacco
Buyers pay \(p^c=(1+\tau)p=1.2p\); sellers receive \(p\); \(p_a=1\). Incomes (at producer prices) are still \(I_C=4p+1\), \(I_D=p+4\). With lump-sum transfers \((T_C,T_D)\), \[
X_{t,C}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{I_C+T_C}{1.2p},\quad
X_{a,C}=\frac{2}{3}(I_C+T_C),\qquad
X_{t,D}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{I_D+T_D}{1.2p},\quad
X_{a,D}=\frac{1}{3}(I_D+T_D).
\]

Market clearing: \(X_{t,C}+X_{t,D}=5\), \(X_{a,C}+X_{a,D}=5\).


(a) Equilibrium conditions, any sum such that \(T_C+T_D=p\)
\[
\frac{(I_C+T_C)/3+2(I_D+T_D)/3}{1.2p}=5,\qquad
\frac{2(I_C+T_C)+(I_D+T_D)}{3}=5,\qquad
T_C+T_D=p.
\]


(b) One revenue-neutral example:

Tax revenue: \(R=\tau\,p\cdot \Omega_t=0.2\,p\cdot 5=p\).
Revenue-neutral: \(T_C+T_D=p\), so any equilibrium condition is revenue-neutral.



(c) Equal rebate transfers
\(T_C=T_D=\tfrac{p}{2}\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{(I_C+p/2)/3+2(I_D+p/2)/3}{\frac{6}{5}p}&=5 \\
\frac{(I_C+p/2)+2(I_D+p/2)}{\frac{6}{5}p}&=15 \\
\frac{I_C+2I_D+\frac{3p}{2}}{\frac{6}{5}p}&=15 \\
I_C+2I_D+\frac{3p}{2}&=18p \\
(4p+1)+2(p+4)+\frac{3p}{2}&=18p \\
6p + \frac{3p}{2} + 9&=18p \\
\frac{12p}{2} + \frac{3p}{2} + 9&=18p \\
\frac{15p}{2}+9&=18p \\
9&=18p - \frac{15p}{2} \\
9&=\frac{36p}{2} - \frac{15p}{2} \\
9&=\frac{21p}{2} \\
p&=\frac{18}{21}=\frac{6}{7}.
\end{aligned}
\] —

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Solution to Exercise 4

Cost of purchasing and income from selling (block prices)
For any \(x\ge 0\), \[
E_A(x)=
\begin{cases}
\bar p_a\,x, & 0\le x\le \bar A,\\[4pt]
\bar p_a\,\bar A+\dfrac{\bar p_a}{2}\,(x-\bar A), & x>\bar A,
\end{cases}
\qquad
E_P(x)=
\begin{cases}
\bar p_p\,x, & 0\le x\le \bar P,\\[4pt]
\bar p_p\,\bar P+\dfrac{\bar p_p}{2}\,(x-\bar P), & x>\bar P.
\end{cases}
\]
Income of \(i\in\{E,F\}\) when endowments are valued at the same schedule: \[
I_i \;=\; E_A(\omega_{iA})+E_P(\omega_{iP}),\qquad
\Omega_A=\omega_{EA}+\omega_{FA},\ \ \Omega_P=\omega_{EP}+\omega_{FP}.
\]


Individual Marshallian demand (Cobb–Douglas, derived from spending)
Cobb–Douglas \(U=X_A^\alpha X_P^{1-\alpha}\) implies the agent targets spendings \[
s_{A,i}=\alpha I_i,\qquad s_{P,i}=(1-\alpha)I_i.
\] Convert spending into quantities by inverting \(E_A,E_P\).

Apples.
If \(s_{A,i}\le \bar p_a\bar A\), all spending is at unit price \(\bar p_a\): \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{s_{A,i}}{\bar p_a}.
\] If \(s_{A,i}>\bar p_a\bar A\), first buy \(\bar A\) units with \(\bar p_a\bar A\), then the remaining spending is \(s_{A,i}-\bar p_a\bar A\) and each extra unit costs \(\bar p_a/2\), so each currency unit buys \(2/\bar p_a\) units: \[
X_{A,i}=\bar A+\frac{s_{A,i}-\bar p_a\bar A}{\bar p_a/2}
\;=\;\bar A+\frac{2}{\bar p_a}\big(s_{A,i}-\bar p_a\bar A\big).
\]
Pears (analogous).
If \(s_{P,i}\le \bar p_p\bar P\), \[
X_{P,i}=\frac{s_{P,i}}{\bar p_p}.
\] If \(s_{P,i}>\bar p_p\bar P\), \[
X_{P,i}=\bar P+\frac{2}{\bar p_p}\big(s_{P,i}-\bar p_p\bar P\big).
\]

Substitute \(s_{A,i}=\alpha I_i\) and \(s_{P,i}=(1-\alpha)I_i\) in each branch.


Market clearing
\[
X_{A,E}+X_{A,F}=\Omega_A,\qquad X_{P,E}+X_{P,F}=\Omega_P.
\]

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Solution to Exercise 5

1–4) Box, budgets, indifference curves, slope

Box \(6\times 6\), initial endowment at \((4,2)\) for \(A\) (hence \((2,4)\) for \(B\)).
Budget lines through the endowment with slope \(-\frac{p_1}{p_2}\).
Indifference curves for \(A\) from \(X_1^\alpha X_2^{1-\alpha}=\bar u\): \[
X_2=\bar u^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}\,X_1^{-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}},
\] which are convex to the origin (diminishing MRS).



5) Equilibrium price ratio and allocation
Let \(p_2=1\), \(p_1=p\). Incomes: \(I_A=4p+2\), \(I_B=2p+4\). Demand for good 1: \(X_{1,A}=\alpha I_A/p\), \(X_{1,B}=\alpha I_B/p\). Clear good 1 (total supply \(6\)): \[
\alpha\Big(\frac{4p+2}{p}+\frac{2p+4}{p}\Big)=6
\ \Rightarrow\
\alpha\Big(6+\frac{6}{p}\Big)=6
\ \Rightarrow\
p=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
\] Then \[
I_A=\frac{2}{1-\alpha},\qquad I_B=\frac{4}{1-\alpha},
\] and allocations \[
X_{1,A}=2,\ X_{2,A}=2;\qquad X_{1,B}=4,\ X_{2,B}=4.
\] By homotheticity, the equilibrium allocation is independent of \(\alpha\) given the symmetric totals \((6,6)\).

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Notes on terminology (kept simple)

Homothetic preferences: if we scale a consumption bundle by any positive factor, the ranking of bundles does not change along that ray (indifference curves are “scaled copies”). Why it matters: income expansion paths are straight lines through the origin, and Marshallian demands are proportional to income. For homothetic preferences, Hicksian and Marshallian coincide at the Marshallian utility level.

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
section: Solution to Exercise 4 (piecewise prices — clear recipe)
text:
Solution to Exercise 4 (piecewise prices — clear recipe)
We convert the block prices into piecewise expenditure functions. For any quantity \(x\) and solve the problem for every case.

Apples: \[
E_A(x)=
\begin{cases}
\bar p_a\,x, & 0\le x\le \bar A,\\[4pt]
\bar p_a\,\bar A+\dfrac{\bar p_a}{2}\,(x-\bar A), & x>\bar A.
\end{cases}
\]
Pears: \[
E_P(x)=
\begin{cases}
\bar p_p\,x, & 0\le x\le \bar P,\\[4pt]
\bar p_p\,\bar P+\dfrac{\bar p_p}{2}\,(x-\bar P), & x>\bar P.
\end{cases}
\]

These encode “first block at full price, extra units at half price”.

(1) Budget and case-by-case Marshallian demand
Step A (income at block prices). Selling at the same schedule, consumer \(i\in\{E,F\}\) has income \[
I_i=E_A(\omega_{iA})+E_P(\omega_{iP}).
\]
Step B (Cobb–Douglas spending shares). With \(U=X_A^\alpha X_P^{1-\alpha}\), the consumer targets \[
\text{spend on apples}=\alpha I_i,\qquad \text{spend on pears}=(1-\alpha)I_i.
\]
Step C (invert “spend \(\to\) quantity” for each good). The inverse of \(E_A\) and \(E_P\) gives quantities from targeted spending \(s\):

Apples quantity from spending \(s_A\): \[
X_{A,i}=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s_A}{\bar p_a}, & s_A\le \bar p_a\bar A,\\[6pt]
\bar A+\dfrac{2}{\bar p_a}\big(s_A-\bar p_a\bar A\big), & s_A> \bar p_a\bar A,
\end{cases}
\qquad s_A:=\alpha I_i.
\]
Pears quantity from spending \(s_P\): \[
X_{P,i}=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s_P}{\bar p_p}, & s_P\le \bar p_p\bar P,\\[6pt]
\bar P+\dfrac{2}{\bar p_p}\big(s_P-\bar p_p\bar P\big), & s_P> \bar p_p\bar P,
\end{cases}
\qquad s_P:=(1-\alpha) I_i.
\]

This is the complete piecewise Marshallian demand (first-block case vs. beyond-first-block case) for each consumer.


(2) Market clearing and equilibrium prices
Let totals be \(\Omega_A=\omega_{EA}+\omega_{FA}\) and \(\Omega_P=\omega_{EP}+\omega_{FP}\). Choose a numeraire (set, e.g., \(\bar p_p=1\)). Prices \((\bar p_a,\bar p_p)\) must solve \[
X_{A,E}(\bar p_a,\bar p_p)+X_{A,F}(\bar p_a,\bar p_p)=\Omega_A,\qquad
X_{P,E}(\bar p_a,\bar p_p)+X_{P,F}(\bar p_a,\bar p_p)=\Omega_P,
\] where \(X_{\cdot,i}\) are the case-by-case formulas above using \(I_i=E_A(\omega_{iA})+E_P(\omega_{iP})\).

Practical recipe: 1. Pick \(\bar p_p=1\) and guess which case (first-block or beyond) applies for each \((i,\text{good})\) by checking the thresholds \(\bar p_a\bar A\) and \(\bar P\) against \(\alpha I_i\) and \((1-\alpha)I_i\). 2. Write the corresponding expressions for \(X_{A,E}+X_{A,F}\) and \(X_{P,E}+X_{P,F}\). 3. Solve the two linear equations for \(\bar p_a\) (and, if not normalized, \(\bar p_p\)). If a guess fails an inequality, switch that term to the other branch and solve again.

Useful closed form when both consumers are beyond the first block for both goods and both totals exceed thresholds (\(\Omega_A>\bar A\), \(\Omega_P>\bar P\) and \(\alpha I_i>\bar p_a\bar A\), \((1-\alpha)I_i>\bar p_p\bar P\) for \(i=E,F\)):
With \(\bar p_p=1\), \[
\bar p_a=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P}{\Omega_A}.
\] Then determine each \(I_i\) from Step A and plug into Step C (using the “beyond-first-block” branch) to get \(X_{A,i},X_{P,i}\).


(3) Equilibrium allocations
Given the equilibrium prices, compute \(I_i\) and then \(X_{A,i},X_{P,i}\) via the case formulas in (1). By construction, \[
X_{A,E}+X_{A,F}=\Omega_A,\qquad X_{P,E}+X_{P,F}=\Omega_P.
\]


(4) Comparative statics in \(\bar A,\bar P\) (intuition made precise)

Raising \(\bar A\) or \(\bar P\) delays the switch to the cheaper second block (more units are charged the higher “first-block” price). For fixed endowments, this tends to reduce quantities at a given price and therefore typically pushes the corresponding equilibrium price up to clear the market—unless totals are so small that the second block would not be reached anyway.
In the “beyond-first-block for everyone” case above, the clean price formula \[
\bar p_a=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P}{\Omega_A}
\] does not depend on \((\bar A,\bar P)\) directly; instead, larger thresholds make it harder for agents to be in that regime. If a threshold becomes large enough, some agents fall into the first-block branch, and the price becomes the solution of the mixed case system in (2).

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Equilibria by aggregate regime
Below, price levels are determined up to a numeraire; relative prices are pinned down. Allocations for each agent follow directly by plugging \(I_i\) into the corresponding branches above.

Case 1: Neither good reaches the second block
\[
\Omega_A\le \bar A,\qquad \Omega_P\le \bar P.
\] Everyone is in the first-block branch for both goods. Then \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{\alpha I_i}{\bar p_a},\qquad X_{P,i}=\frac{(1-\alpha)I_i}{\bar p_p}.
\] Market clearing implies \[
\frac{\alpha(I_E+I_F)}{\bar p_a}=\Omega_A,\qquad \frac{(1-\alpha)(I_E+I_F)}{\bar p_p}=\Omega_P,
\] so the relative price is \[
\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P}{\Omega_A}.
\]


Case 2: Only apples reach the second block
\[
\Omega_A>\bar A,\qquad \Omega_P\le \bar P.
\] Apples: both agents use the beyond-first-block branch
Pears: both agents use the first-block branch. Then \[
X_{A,i}=\bar A+\frac{2}{\bar p_a}\big(\alpha I_i-\bar p_a\bar A\big)
\;=\;\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}I_i-\bar A,
\qquad
X_{P,i}=\frac{(1-\alpha)I_i}{\bar p_p}.
\] Aggregate clearing: \[
\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar A=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}(I_E+I_F)=\Omega_P.
\] Hence \[
\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}
=\frac{2\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P}{\Omega_A+2\bar A}.
\]


Case 3: Only pears reach the second block
\[
\Omega_A\le \bar A,\qquad \Omega_P>\bar P.
\] Apples: first-block branch
Pears: beyond-first-block branch. Then \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{\alpha I_i}{\bar p_a},\qquad
X_{P,i}=\bar P+\frac{2}{\bar p_p}\big((1-\alpha) I_i-\bar p_p\bar P\big)
=\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}I_i-\bar P.
\] Aggregate clearing: \[
\frac{\alpha}{\bar p_a}(I_E+I_F)=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar P=\Omega_P.
\] Hence \[
\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}
=\frac{\alpha}{2(1-\alpha)}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P+2\bar P}{\Omega_A}.
\]


Case 4: Both goods reach the second block (deep interior)
\[
\Omega_A>\bar A,\qquad \Omega_P>\bar P.
\] Both agents use the beyond-first-block branch for both goods. Then \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}I_i-\bar A,\qquad
X_{P,i}=\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}I_i-\bar P.
\] Aggregate clearing: \[
\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar A=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar P=\Omega_P.
\] Divide the two equations to eliminate \(I_E+I_F\) and obtain the relative price: \[
\boxed{\ \frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P+2\bar P}{\Omega_A+2\bar A}\ }.
\]

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Equilibrium allocations (all cases)
Once \((\bar p_a,\bar p_p)\) are fixed (up to a numeraire), compute \(I_i=E_A(\omega_{iA})+E_P(\omega_{iP})\) and then plug into the appropriate branch:

First-block branch: \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{\alpha I_i}{\bar p_a},\qquad X_{P,i}=\frac{(1-\alpha) I_i}{\bar p_p}.
\]
Beyond-first-block branch: \[
X_{A,i}=\bar A+\frac{2}{\bar p_a}\big(\alpha I_i-\bar p_a\bar A\big)
=\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}I_i-\bar A,
\] \[
X_{P,i}=\bar P+\frac{2}{\bar p_p}\big((1-\alpha) I_i-\bar p_p\bar P\big)
=\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}I_i-\bar P.
\]

These allocations satisfy \(X_{A,E}+X_{A,F}=\Omega_A\) and \(X_{P,E}+X_{P,F}=\Omega_P\) in each case.

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Comparative statics in \((\bar A,\bar P)\)
In any regime in which a good uses the second block in equilibrium, its relative price moves with the corresponding threshold: \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \bar A}\left(\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}\right)>0\quad\text{when apples use the second block},\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial \bar P}\left(\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}\right)<0\quad\text{when pears use the second block}.
\] The closed-form expressions above (Cases 2–4) show this directly.

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
section: Equilibrium by aggregate regime (prices up to a numeraire)
text:
Equilibrium by aggregate regime (prices up to a numeraire)
Below, we present closed forms for the relative price and the implied allocations when the aggregate economy falls in one of four quantity regimes. In each case, compute \(I_i\) from endowments, plug into the branch formulas above, and the allocations will sum to \((\Omega_A,\Omega_P)\).

Case 1: Neither good uses the second block
\[
\Omega_A\le \bar A,\qquad \Omega_P\le \bar P.
\] All agents are in the first-block branch for both goods: \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{\alpha I_i}{\bar p_a},\qquad
X_{P,i}=\frac{(1-\alpha) I_i}{\bar p_p}.
\] Clearing implies \[
\frac{\alpha(I_E+I_F)}{\bar p_a}=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{(1-\alpha)(I_E+I_F)}{\bar p_p}=\Omega_P
\ \Rightarrow\
\boxed{\ \frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot\frac{\Omega_P}{\Omega_A}\ }.
\]


Case 2: Only apples use the second block
\[
\Omega_A>\bar A,\qquad \Omega_P\le \bar P.
\] Apples beyond-first-block, pears first-block. Using the spending-to-quantity conversion: \[
X_{A,i}=\bar A+\frac{2}{\bar p_a}\big(\alpha I_i-\bar p_a\bar A\big)
=\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}I_i-\bar A,\qquad
X_{P,i}=\frac{(1-\alpha) I_i}{\bar p_p}.
\] Summing and clearing: \[
\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar A=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{1-\alpha}{\bar p_p}(I_E+I_F)=\Omega_P,
\] hence \[
\boxed{\ \frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}
=\frac{2\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P}{\Omega_A+2\bar A}\ }.
\]


Case 3: Only pears use the second block
\[
\Omega_A\le \bar A,\qquad \Omega_P>\bar P.
\] Apples first-block, pears beyond-first-block: \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{\alpha I_i}{\bar p_a},\qquad
X_{P,i}=\bar P+\frac{2}{\bar p_p}\big((1-\alpha) I_i-\bar p_p\bar P\big)
=\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}I_i-\bar P.
\] Summing and clearing: \[
\frac{\alpha}{\bar p_a}(I_E+I_F)=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar P=\Omega_P,
\] so \[
\boxed{\ \frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}
=\frac{\alpha}{2(1-\alpha)}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P+2\bar P}{\Omega_A}\ }.
\]


Case 4: Both goods use the second block (deep interior)
\[
\Omega_A>\bar A,\qquad \Omega_P>\bar P.
\] Both beyond-first-block: \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}I_i-\bar A,\qquad
X_{P,i}=\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}I_i-\bar P.
\] Summing and clearing: \[
\frac{2\alpha}{\bar p_a}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar A=\Omega_A,\qquad
\frac{2(1-\alpha)}{\bar p_p}(I_E+I_F)-2\bar P=\Omega_P,
\] giving \[
\boxed{\ \frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot \frac{\Omega_P+2\bar P}{\Omega_A+2\bar A}\ }.
\]



Equilibrium allocations (all regimes)

Compute \(I_i=E_A(\omega_{iA})+E_P(\omega_{iP})\) using the block-price cost functions above.

Use the appropriate branch for each good:


First-block branch: \[
X_{A,i}=\frac{\alpha I_i}{\bar p_a},\qquad
X_{P,i}=\frac{(1-\alpha) I_i}{\bar p_p}.
\]
Beyond-first-block branch: \[
X_{A,i}=\bar A+\frac{2}{\bar p_a}\big(\alpha I_i-\bar p_a\bar A\big),\qquad
X_{P,i}=\bar P+\frac{2}{\bar p_p}\big((1-\alpha) I_i-\bar p_p\bar P\big).
\]

These allocations satisfy \(X_{A,E}+X_{A,F}=\Omega_A\) and \(X_{P,E}+X_{P,F}=\Omega_P\) by construction.



Comparative statics in \(\bar A,\bar P\)
When a good uses the second block in equilibrium, the marginal price relevant for most purchased units is \(\bar p/2\), and the relative price adjusts so that, holding endowments fixed, \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \bar A}\left(\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}\right)>0
\quad\text{if apples use the second block},\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial \bar P}\left(\frac{\bar p_a}{\bar p_p}\right)<0
\quad\text{if pears use the second block}.
\]
